title: FAQ:
title_short: V04 · How Do Hospitals Work With Watsi?
headline: Watsi never walks in with a solution: it vets each hospital, funds each patient's care, and walks alongside them for years, like the Uganda clinic that grew from a shed under a jackfruit tree into a solar-powered maternity center.
story: Mackinnon answers one question to camera: how do hospitals work with Watsi? It is a real partnership. Watsi vets every partner, then the flow is simple: a patient who needs care, a local Watsi rep, the case, the story, the payment, the update to every donor.

Then the proof: a partner hospital in Uganda that started as a shed under a jackfruit tree and is now a solar-powered maternity center. “We could not have done this without Watsi.” The pictures for that story come from Uganda, not Medellín.
do: Open on frame 1 with the question as top text, over a walking shot from Uganda.
Show the Watsi rep at work on “the local Watsi rep” (Jimmy's B-roll, Uganda).
Use Uganda footage for every place she describes: the clinic, the rep, the birthing centre.
Keep her natural pauses and her order.
dont: No Smile Train footage or logo anywhere. Replace every shot that shows it.
No Medellín B-roll where the words describe partners or Uganda.
No extra animation. Only the graphics in this plan.
No reused hospital entrance or patient sequence from the Dr Ana Maria, Caldwell and Mackinnon cuts.
Do not post the same week as V08 (the jackfruit story repeats).

rows.visual: Her face on “We vet”. On “their reputation with the community” cut to FX3_0036.MP4 00:06.0 to 00:09.0: patients wait in a Uganda clinic, a nurse behind them (visual.json, check on scrub). voice.quote: We vet every medical partner carefully, their reputation with the community, their trust, their quality of care, their capacity to really track and report transparently. And this process can take months.

rows.visual: Her face on “Once we're working together”. Then FX3_0122.MP4 00:05.0 to 00:09.0, a man in a white shirt talks with a woman at a desk. On “submits the case” cut to FX3_0116.MP4 00:03.0 to 00:06.0, the rep writes at a desk with a laptop. Back to her face on “We review it”. Do not name Jimmy on screen.
rows.motion: Captions only. Keep it simple: no animation on this row.

voice.quote: Once we're working together, the flow goes like this. The hospital has a patient who needs care but can't afford the treatment. So they're introduced to the local Watsi rep who learns more about the family and their need and provides the information and consent and submits the case to Watsi. We review it, get it ready, and share the story.

rows.visual: Her face for the payment lines. On “we always share the patient's update” cut to a screen recording of a real patient update on watsi.org on a phone. Record it fresh. Never fake a page. Back to her face for the end of the line.

voice.quote: When the treatment's complete and the hospital has shared the outcomes, we send them a payment. Even if we're still fundraising for the care, we send the payment. And we always share the patient's update with every single person who donated.

rows.sfx: One soft UI tap on the cut to the phone.

shots.screen: real patient update on watsi.org, recorded fresh

rows.visual: Her face. This is the point of the answer, so the face is the strongest picture. One 106% punch-in on “and most importantly”.

voice.quote: The hospital gets reliable funding, donors get real accountability, and most importantly, patients get the care they need.

rows.visual: Her face on “And over time”. On “a shed under a jackfruit tree” cut to the jackfruit tree from the Uganda shoot: B-roll TBD on scrub (Atdhe: there is footage of this tree from the latest Uganda shoot; look in Uganda Footage ▸ B-Roll and Drone). voice.quote: And over time, that partnership builds. I remember one of our partner hospitals in Uganda. It simply started as a shed under a jackfruit tree selling malaria medicine. [00:43.2] We review it, get it ready, and share the story.
[00:45.7] When the treatment's complete and the hospital has shared the outcomes, we send them a payment.
[00:50.6] Even if we're still fundraising for the care, we send the payment.
[00:53.9] And we always share the patient's update with every single person who donated.
[00:58.3] The hospital gets reliable funding, donors get real accountability, and most importantly, patients get the care they need.
